title: A Tree Cut Down
sum: Nebuchadnezzar writes to every people in his empire to tell how the Most High humbled him. He dreamed of a huge tree that sheltered every living thing. A watcher, a holy one, came down from heaven and ordered it chopped down, leaving only a stump bound with iron and bronze. His magicians and diviners could not explain the dream. Daniel could, and the meaning was grim: the tree is the king, who will be driven out from among people to live like an animal for seven periods, until he knows that the Most High is ruler over the kingdom of humankind (4:25).

Daniel urged him to break with his sins by doing what is right and being kind to the poor (4:27). Twelve months later, as the king looked over Babylon and boasted that he had built it by his own power, a voice fell from heaven and the sentence took effect that very hour. At the end of the time he lifted his eyes, his reason returned, and he praised the King of heaven (4:34-37). The chapter is told as the king's own letter, a confession in the mouth of the empire's most famous ruler.
readings: Read as the king's own history

On the traditional view the letter preserves a real event late in Nebuchadnezzar's reign, kept in Daniel's book in the king's own voice. Babylonian records for his last decades are thin, and a Greek writer, Abydenus (quoted in Eusebius), tells of the king seized by a god on his palace roof and then vanishing. The Old Greek's date, the king's eighteenth year, would put the story near the fall of Jerusalem.
Read as a court tale shaped by the story of Nabonidus

Critical readers see a court tale in the form of a royal letter, in which a proud foreign king learns what Israel's God can do. The best-known ancient parallel is about the last king of Babylon, Nabonidus, who spent about ten years away at Teima in Arabia. An Aramaic prayer from Qumran (4Q242) has him struck with an illness for seven years until a Jewish diviner forgave his sin. On this view the story passed from one king to the other, and the Old Greek and Aramaic versions show it was told in more than one form.
Read as a lesson about pride

Whatever its origin, the chapter states its point three times: the Most High is ruler over the kingdom of humankind and gives it to whomever he pleases (4:17, 25, 32). The tree, the stump and the animal's heart turn a king into a picture of every proud power in the book. The first beast of chapter 7 is given a human heart (7:4), as if it learned this lesson.

views.H: Nebuchadnezzar II ruled 605-562 BC and rebuilt Babylon on a grand scale (4:30), and nothing in Babylonian records confirms or denies an illness. The sixth-century reading takes the story as his, late in his reign; the late-date reading takes it as a tale about a Babylonian king, with the Nabonidus years at Teima (about 553-543 BC) as its likely source. Both agree that the chapter is about Babylon's most powerful ruler learning that he is a creature.
views.C: Most critical scholars see chapters 1-6 as older court tales (a genre W. Lee Humphreys called the 'diaspora court tale') gathered in Aramaic and joined to the visions by about 165 BC. Chapter 4 shows the tales were told in different forms, since the Old Greek differs greatly. The Persian loanwords and the confusion between Nebuchadnezzar and Nabonidus are, for them, signs of a later author; defenders of an early date answer that the Aramaic and the court details fit the sixth century.
views.J: Rashi, following Rabbi Tanhuma (Mishpatim 4), reads the boast of 4:30 as the moment the king ended the feeding of the poor that Daniel's advice had begun: he heard the poor crying at his door and said he would feed them no more (Rashi on Aramaic 4:27, English 4:30). So the chapter links pride to charity. Jeremiah calls Nebuchadnezzar God's servant (Jeremiah 27:6), and Jewish tradition treats him as an instrument who overreached.
views.X: Christian readers have taken Nebuchadnezzar's fall and restoration as a warning against pride and a picture of repentance. Jerome's Latin of 4:27 ('redeem your sins with alms') made the verse a text for almsgiving. The great tree that shelters the birds was read with Jesus's parable of the mustard seed (Mark 4:32), which uses the same picture for the kingdom of God.
views.F: Some who read Daniel for the end see Nebuchadnezzar's pride as the pattern for the final ruler of 7:25. Some historicist readers have counted the 'seven times' as 2,520 years (seven times 360 days, each day a year), and Jehovah's Witnesses count them from 607 BC to AD 1914 (Insight on the Scriptures), a date for Jerusalem's fall that most historians reject (586 BC). Most readers who take the periods literally read them as years of the king's own life.

deep.h: Which witnesses this site checked, for chapters 4-7
deep.b:
The Plain is translated from the Aramaic of the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008), verse by verse from a word-for-word rendering. The Dead Sea Scrolls were read in the transcriptions of Martin Abegg, James Bowley and Edward Cook (ETCBC dss): 4QDan-a (4Q112), 4QDan-b (4Q113) and 4QDan-d (4Q115) preserve parts of these chapters. Their copying is dated to the second or first century BC, as reported by Ulrich in Discoveries in the Judaean Desert 16. Restored words are never cited as a scroll's reading. 1QDan-a and 1QDan-b and 6QpapDan do not contain these chapters. The Old Greek was read in Swete's edition, which prints it from Codex Chisianus (88), and Theodotion in the same edition; the critical Göttingen edition (Ziegler) is cited as reported by Collins. Papyrus 967 of the Old Greek, which orders the book 1-4, 7-8, 5-6 and then 9-12, is likewise reported by its editors and was not read here. Rashi's comments on Daniel 4:26-27 and 34, 5:1, and 7:4-9, 13, 24 and 25 were read on Sefaria in the Judaica Press translation. Talmudic, midrashic and church-father passages are cited as reported in the sources named in each note, as are the Nabonidus Chronicle, Herodotus, Xenophon and the Prayer of Nabonidus.

The variants list the places where the witnesses differ in meaning. Spelling differences, which are many in the scrolls, are not listed.

Daniel 2:4b-7:28 is written in Aramaic, the common language of the Babylonian and Persian empires, and the rest of the book is Hebrew. The Plain keeps Aramaic forms recognizable in notes (malkuta, 'kingdom'; elah, 'God'; qaddishin, 'holy ones'). Scholars have noticed that chapters 2-7 are built as a chiasm: the four kingdoms (2 and 7), a deliverance from death (3 and 6), and proud kings humbled (4 and 5), as A. Lenglet showed in 1972. Why the author switched languages is unknown. The language itself is debated in the date question: defenders of the sixth century say it is close to the Official Aramaic of the Persian empire, while critics compare it with the later Aramaic of Qumran and see Persian and Greek loanwords. This part adds the Persian words raz (4:9), dat (6:5) and achashdarpan (6:1).

echoes: Ezekiel 31:3-14; Ezekiel 17:22-24; Isaiah 10:33-11:1; Job 14:7-9; Mark 4:30-32; Jeremiah 27:6-7; Psalm 92:12-15; Deuteronomy 28:28; Revelation 18:2

settings.what: Nebuchadnezzar's letter to the whole empire
settings.by: King Nebuchadnezzar, as the text presents him
settings.to: 'All peoples, nations and languages who live in all the earth', that is, every subject of his empire
settings.when: After his recovery, once his reason and his kingdom were restored (4:36)
settings.why: A public confession: the king tells the signs God did to him so that the whole empire will know the Most High rules, and warns every proud ruler by his own example. The greeting also makes it an official document of the empire.
settings.readers: Later Jewish readers, in exile and in the diaspora, heard a world ruler confess what they believed; Christians read it with Daniel 2:47 and 6:26 as a pattern of the nations coming to God.
views: Jews in Babylon and Persia would take heart that the empire's greatest king had acknowledged their God, and that its rulers could be humbled.
Jews under Greek rulers, and later under Antiochus IV, needed the story of a king who defied heaven and was cut down, since Antiochus claimed the title 'God made manifest' (Epiphanes).

settings.what: The king tells Daniel his dream
settings.to: Daniel (Belteshazzar), called in at the end, after the Babylonian wise men had failed
settings.when: In the palace, after a night of fearful visions
settings.why: The king wants a meaning for the dream, since it troubles him and his experts cannot supply one. He asks Daniel because 'a spirit of the holy gods' is in him. The request puts Daniel in the same position as in chapter 2: the one who knows what the court cannot.
settings.readers: Readers see again that interpretation belongs to God, a point repeated in chapters 2, 5 and 7.

settings.to: King Nebuchadnezzar, privately, in the palace
settings.when: After an hour of silence, as Daniel took in how severe the sentence was
settings.why: Daniel must tell the king that he will be cast out, and does so with a courtier's wish that the dream apply to the king's enemies. Then he offers advice meant to avert the sentence: break with sin by doing what is right and show mercy to the poor. It is a prophet's warning with a way out, as in Jonah.
settings.readers: The call to justice and to the poor is the verse early Christian readers took up for almsgiving, and Jewish readers for charity (tsedaqah).

settings.to: Nebuchadnezzar, on his palace roof, while the boast was still on his lips
settings.why: The sentence is now carried out. The voice repeats the words of the dream and Daniel's interpretation in the second person, so that no one can say he was not warned.

title: The Writing on the Wall
sum: King Belshazzar gives a banquet for a thousand nobles, and sends for the gold and silver vessels that his father Nebuchadnezzar carried off from the temple in Jerusalem. As the guests drink from them and sing the praises of gods of gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood and stone, the fingers of a human hand appear and write on the plaster of the wall. The king's color changes, his legs give way, and his wise men cannot read the writing or say what it means, until the queen remembers Daniel.

Daniel refuses the king's gifts and reminds him how pride destroyed Nebuchadnezzar. He charges Belshazzar with using the vessels of God's house and praising lifeless gods, and then reads four words: mene, mene, tekel, parsin. God has counted out your kingdom and finished it; you were put on a scale and found lacking; your kingdom is divided and handed to the Medes and Persians. Daniel is dressed in purple and proclaimed third ruler. That same night Belshazzar is killed, and Darius the Mede receives the kingdom.
readings: Read as the last night of Babylon

On the traditional view the chapter is an eyewitness-based account of the night Babylon fell to Cyrus in October 539 BC, and it is accurate in a detail that later writers forgot: Belshazzar, the crown prince, held power while his father was away at Teima. Greek writers (Herodotus, Xenophon) agree that the city fell during a feast.
Read as a tale of sacrilege and judgment

Critical readers read the story as a court tale of a king who profanes sacred things and is undone, paired with chapter 4 in the chiasm of chapters 2-7. Belshazzar's offense is the opposite of Nebuchadnezzar's: he knew the lesson of chapter 4 and ignored it (5:22). The author's vagueness about Belshazzar's family and about Darius the Mede shows, they say, that he wrote from tradition, not records.
Read as a message for those who saw the temple profaned

Antiochus IV took the temple's vessels in 169 BC (1 Maccabees 1:21-24) and defiled the temple in 167. For readers who date the book then, a story in which a king who drinks from the vessels of God's house is killed that night is a promise that God judges such kings.

views.H: Cyrus's army took Babylon without a battle in October 539 BC, as the Nabonidus Chronicle says, while Belshazzar, Nabonidus's son, had been running the city and army. The vessels came to Babylon in 597 and 586 BC (2 Kings 24:13; 25:13-15), and Cyrus gave back 5,400 in 538 BC (Ezra 1:7-11). The late-date reading sees the same events, remembered at some distance.
views.C: Belshazzar was not Nebuchadnezzar's son, he was never formally king, and the real Babylonian succession was Amel-Marduk, Neriglissar, Labashi-Marduk, Nabonidus. Daniel's order of Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, Darius the Mede fits the author's four-kingdom scheme (Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece) better than history. Defenders reply that 'son' covers descendant, and that hardly any later writer knew of Belshazzar's role at all (Baruch 1:11-12 names him).
views.J: Rashi writes that Belshazzar was Nebuchadnezzar's son who reigned after Evil-merodach, and that, as the Yosippon says, he fought Darius and Cyrus by day, won, and made his feast that evening, as Isaiah had foretold; the enemies returned during the feast and took the city (Rashi on Daniel 5:1). Jewish tradition links the feast to Isaiah 21:5 and to the vessels of the temple.
views.X: Christian readers have taken the fall of Babylon as the end of the first kingdom of Daniel 2 and 7, and Revelation takes up 'Babylon the great' and its fall (Revelation 18:2, 21). The writing on the wall has become a figure of God's verdict on proud power.
views.F: For readers who look to the end, the feast and the fall are a pattern of the last judgment on the world city in Revelation 17-18, where the harlot Babylon drinks from a golden cup and falls in an hour.

deep.b: Babylonian texts name Bel-shar-usur ('Bel, protect the king') as the eldest son of Nabonidus, and they show him as crown prince. The Nabonidus Chronicle records that in the seventh to eleventh years of Nabonidus the king was in Teima and the crown prince, with the army, was in Akkad. The Verse Account of Nabonidus says the king entrusted the army and the kingship to his eldest son. Business documents of the time swear oaths by both the king and the crown prince, a rare honor. No Babylonian text calls Belshazzar 'king', and Herodotus, Xenophon and Berossus do not name him (Berossus, quoted by Josephus, gives Nabonidus the last place); Daniel's 'king' therefore reflects real power more than title. The date of Belshazzar's death is not given in the Chronicle. See the topic on Belshazzar.

echoes: Isaiah 21:1-10; Isaiah 13:17-22; Jeremiah 51:39, 57; Jeremiah 27:7; 2 Kings 25:13-15; Ezra 1:7-11; Psalm 115:4-8; Exodus 31:18; Revelation 18:2, 21

settings.to: King Belshazzar and his nobles, in the banquet hall
settings.when: After the king's wise men had failed to read the writing
settings.why: She calms the terrified king and tells him of a man who served his 'father' Nebuchadnezzar, so that Daniel is called when no one else can help. She is the only person at the feast who remembers.
settings.readers: Readers learn that Daniel has been forgotten at court for years, which shows how quickly a ruler's memory of God's servants fades.

settings.to: Daniel, brought in before the king and his nobles
settings.when: The same night, after the queen's advice and after the wise men had failed
settings.why: The king questions Daniel as a stranger ('Are you that Daniel?'), repeats what he has heard of him, and offers purple, a gold chain and third place in the kingdom for reading the writing. He speaks as a frightened ruler who has just seen his own experts fail, and he offers rewards he can no longer keep.
settings.readers: Readers see a king who must ask an exile from the conquered people to save him, and who does not remember the man his 'father' had set over the wise men.
views: The exile community heard how their own member was summoned to the throne of the empire that held them.
Jews under Antiochus IV heard how a pagan king's offered rewards mean nothing when God's verdict is already written.

settings.what: Daniel's rebuke and reading of the writing
settings.to: King Belshazzar and his thousand nobles, at the banquet
settings.when: The night of the feast, in the hour the writing appeared
settings.why: Daniel refuses rewards because the message is a judgment, then charges the king with ignoring what he knew of Nebuchadnezzar's fall and with dishonoring the vessels and the God who holds his breath. The reading of three words announces that the kingdom is finished, tested and divided. It is a prophecy delivered as an interpretation.
settings.readers: The exiles who treasured the memory of the temple's plunder read here that God had not forgotten the vessels. Later, readers under Antiochus IV would see the same judgment on a king who took them again.
views: The first hearers were the exile community under Babylon and then Persia, assured that Babylon's end was set by God and near.
The first hearers were Jews in Antiochus's day, for whom a pagan king's fall for profaning the temple's vessels was a promise about the king they feared.

settings.what: The reward, the king's death and the change of rule
settings.by: King Belshazzar (the command), then the narrator
settings.to: Daniel and the court; the reader
settings.when: The same night, as the Medes and Persians take the kingdom
settings.why: Belshazzar keeps his promise and honors Daniel even after hearing a death sentence. Then in two lines the narrator reports the king's death and the transfer of rule to Darius the Mede. The story gives no battle and no details, only the verdict fulfilled.
settings.readers: Later readers saw the end of the first kingdom of Daniel 2 and 7, and Jews and Christians alike took the quick fall as proof that God sets up and removes kings (compare 4:17).
views: The exiles heard of Babylon's fall as the end of their captors' rule, in the days of Cyrus.
Jews of 167-164 BC heard that a king who profaned the temple's vessels fell the same night, a promise about their own persecutor.

title: In the Lions' Den
sum: Darius the Mede sets one hundred twenty satraps over his kingdom and three overseers over them, and Daniel soon outshines them all. The others, unable to find a fault in his work, trap him through his faith: they persuade the king to sign a ban that for thirty days no one may ask any god or person for anything except the king, on pain of the lions' den. The law of the Medes and Persians cannot be changed. Daniel goes home, opens his upstairs windows toward Jerusalem, and prays three times a day as always.

The plotters catch him praying, and the king, who tries all day to save him, must give the order. A stone is laid over the den and sealed. The king spends the night without food, hurries to the den at dawn, and calls out. Daniel answers that God sent his angel and shut the lions' mouths, because he was found innocent. Daniel is lifted out unharmed, his accusers and their families are thrown in, and Darius writes to the whole world that the God of Daniel is the living God whose kingdom never ends.
readings: Read as a story of faithful prayer under a decree

The center of the story is a single act: Daniel prays as he always did, in the open, toward Jerusalem. The decree turns an ordinary habit into a crime. The story asks what a person does when obeying the state would mean giving up prayer, and it answers with Daniel's quiet refusal.
Read as a court tale of envy and rescue

The pattern is the same as Joseph in Genesis 39 and Esther's Mordecai: a faithful official, envious rivals, a trap in the law, a rescue and a reversal. It is paired with chapter 3 (a decree, a test of loyalty, a miraculous rescue, a royal confession) in the chiasm of 2-7.
Read as a story for people under a ban on worship

Readers who date the book to Antiochus IV see in the thirty-day ban a picture of his decrees against Jewish observance (1 Maccabees 1:41-50). The story then encouraged those who kept the law at the risk of death, and the story of Daniel's escape was remembered in Mattathias's last words (1 Maccabees 2:60).

views.H: Cyrus took Babylon in 539 BC, and Persian rule was by satraps, with decrees sealed in the king's name. The ban fits no known Persian practice, though it needs only a flattered king; the identity of Darius the Mede (see 5:31) remains the main puzzle. The late-date reading sets the story in the memory of the Persian period or the Hellenistic persecution.
views.C: Most critical scholars take 6 as a legend that parallels 3, with Persian court details (satraps, the unchangeable law, Medes before Persians) built from tradition. The Old Greek tells a shorter story with two plotters and a different decree, which shows it circulated in several forms. The names, the count of satraps and the Median kingdom are, for them, signs of a writer later than the Persian period.
views.J: Daniel became a model of faithful prayer: toward Jerusalem (the Mishnah, Berakhot 4:5-6, tells those abroad to face the Land and the temple) and at fixed hours (Psalm 55:17). The story belongs to the Jewish tradition of those who risked death for the law, with Daniel's three friends in chapter 3.
views.X: Hebrews 11:33-34 lists those who 'shut the mouths of lions' among the heroes of faith. In early Christian art Daniel standing among the lions, arms raised in prayer, is one of the commonest figures in catacomb paintings and on sarcophagi, a sign of rescue from death. Readers also noticed the sealed stone and the dawn visit, which recall the tomb of Jesus (Matthew 27:60-66).
views.F: Readers who expect a final ruler who demands exclusive worship (Revelation 13:15) see Darius's ban as a pattern of that demand, and Daniel's refusal as the pattern for the faithful in the last days.

deep.h: The furnace and the den: a pair
deep.b: Chapters 3 and 6 mirror each other. In both, officials denounce Jews who stay loyal to their God against a royal decree. The king is distressed, the Jews are thrown into a place of death, an angel saves them (3:28; 6:22), the accusers die (3:22; 6:24), and the king praises the God who saved them (3:28-29; 6:25-27). The mirror is part of the chiasm A-B-C-C'-B'-A' of chapters 2-7. In the Old Greek chapter 6 is shorter and the plot is the work of two young men; the Greek addition Bel and the Dragon adds a second night in the den (see the variant at 6:28).

echoes: Daniel 3; Genesis 39; Esther 3:8; Esther 8:8; Psalm 34:7; Psalm 91:11-13; Psalm 7:15-16; Hebrews 11:33-34; 1 Maccabees 2:60; 2 Timothy 4:17; Matthew 27:60-66; 1 Kings 8:48-49

settings.what: The officials' proposal of a ban
settings.by: The overseers, prefects, satraps, counselors and governors, speaking together
settings.when: After they failed to find a fault in Daniel's work for the kingdom (6:4)
settings.why: They ask for a thirty-day ban on prayer to any god or person except the king, saying it was agreed by all. The king, flattered, signs. They hide that Daniel is the target, and they press the king with the law that cannot be undone (6:8), so that the king's own pride will do the killing.
settings.readers: Later readers saw how an edict can be used to trap the faithful, whether under Persia, Antiochus, or later rulers.
views: Jews living under Persia saw how a law can be turned on a person of faith.
Jews facing Antiochus's decrees read a story of a ban that put faithful worship on trial and then failed.

settings.to: His God, in his upstairs room with the windows open toward Jerusalem
settings.when: Three times a day, and now just after he learned the ban was signed
settings.why: He prays and gives thanks as he always did. The point is that he does not hide or change anything. The text never says what he asked for; it says only that he prayed, thanked and begged for mercy (6:11).
settings.readers: Jews and Christians have kept the pattern of daily prayer toward Jerusalem and the thanks that goes with it; the Didache tells Christians to pray three times a day.

settings.what: The king's struggle, the sealed den and the dawn question
settings.by: King Darius, as the narrator reports him, with the officials' second speech (6:15)
settings.to: The officials, then Daniel at the mouth of the den
settings.when: From the day of the arrest through the sleepless night to first light
settings.why: The king is caught by his own law: he labors until sundown to free Daniel, the officials remind him that no royal ban can be changed (6:15), and he gives the order. He voices a hope (6:16), spends the night fasting, and at dawn calls out in pain, 'Was your God able to rescue you?' The question echoes Nebuchadnezzar's in 3:15.
settings.readers: Readers see a ruler who is powerless against the law he signed, and who is moved to hope by the faith of the man he condemns.
views: Jews living under Persian kings would see in Darius a kindly king bound by court and custom, and still helpless.
Jews facing Antiochus's decrees heard of a king who regretted a ban that could not be undone and learned that God can break the sealed den.

settings.when: After a night among the lions
settings.why: He greets the king courteously, states that God sent his angel, and says he was found innocent before God and before the king. He does not deny that he prayed. He claims innocence before God, whose angel saved him, and says that by praying he did the king no harm.

settings.to: All peoples, nations and languages in his realm
settings.when: After the rescue and the punishment of the plotters
settings.why: As Nebuchadnezzar did after the furnace (3:29) and after his recovery (4:1-3), the king orders reverence for the God of Daniel, who saves and does signs and wonders. The decree reverses the earlier one: a king who forbade prayer now commands fear of Daniel's God.
settings.readers: Readers in exile and under later empires could see a foreign king confess the living God, and the book gives such confessions at the end of chapters 2, 3, 4 and 6.
views: The decree shows the exiles that their God's rescue is known to the world.
The decree set the model of a king who honors God, in contrast to Antiochus.

title: Four Beasts and One Like a Son of Man
sum: In Belshazzar's first year Daniel sees a vision at night. The four winds of heaven whip up the great sea, and four beasts climb out of it: a lion with eagle's wings, a bear raised on one side with three ribs in its mouth, a leopard with four wings and four heads, and a dreadful fourth beast with iron teeth and ten horns. A little horn with a human's eyes and a mouth that speaks big words uproots three of the horns. Then thrones are set, the Ancient of Days takes his seat in white, a stream of fire pours from his presence, thousands upon thousands serve him, the court sits and books are opened. The fourth beast is killed, the others lose their rule, and one like a son of man comes with the clouds of heaven to the Ancient of Days. To him are given rule, honor and a kingdom that all peoples will serve and that will never be destroyed.

Daniel, terrified, asks one of those standing by. The beasts are four kings; the holy ones of the Most High will receive the kingdom and hold it forever. About the fourth beast the angel says more: its kingdom will devour the earth, ten kings will rise from it, and another will come after them, speak against the Most High, wear out the holy ones and try to change the times and the law, for a time, times and half a time. Then the court will sit, his rule will be taken away, and the kingdom and the greatness of all the kingdoms under heaven will be given to the people of the holy ones of the Most High. Daniel keeps the matter in his heart.
readings: Read as the story of Antiochus IV

The critical majority read the four beasts as Babylon, Media, Persia and Greece. Many conservatives, including Calvin and Hengstenberg, hold this reading of the little horn of chapter 8, though not of chapter 7. The little horn is Antiochus IV Epiphanes (175-164 BC), who banned the Sabbath and the offerings and set up the abomination in the temple (1 Maccabees 1:41-64). The holy ones who receive the kingdom are the persecuted faithful or the angels who stand for them, and the time, times and half a time is the three-odd years of the persecution.
Read as Rome and the end

Jerome, Hippolytus, Rashi and most Christian interpreters read the four beasts as Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome. The little horn is a Roman ruler (Rashi says Titus), the Antichrist at the end of the age (Hippolytus, Cyril of Jerusalem and the futurists), or the papacy (Protestant historicists). The one like a son of man is the Messiah, and for Christians, Jesus.
Read as a vision of the heavenly court

Whatever the identifications, the vision moves from earth to heaven and back: the sea and its monsters, the court of the Ancient of Days, a human figure on the clouds, and the explanation by an angel. Its center is 7:9-14, the court scene, which is why scholars call it the book's first apocalypse, with a heavenly view of history that kings cannot see and a kingdom no beast can hold.

views.H: On the sixth-century view, the vision of 553 BC foretells Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece and Rome, and the final kingdom of God. On the Maccabean view it was completed in 167-164 BC, shortly before Antiochus's death, and promises the persecuted that the horn will be removed and the holy ones will receive the kingdom, which in the Hasmonean victory they partly did (1 Maccabees 4:36-59). Both place the vision in the Aramaic frame of chapters 2-7.
views.C: For most critical scholars chapter 7 is the pivot of the book: the Aramaic frame closes with an apocalypse, and Hebrew chapters 8-12 repeat and extend it. They read the beasts as four Near Eastern empires (Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece), the horn as Antiochus IV, the one like a son of man as a symbol or an angel (Michael) and the holy ones as Israel or its angelic guardians. The Old Greek's differences (7:13, 27) show early readers already disagreed on the figure.
views.J: Rashi reads the four beasts as Babylon, Persia, Greece (Antiochus) and Rome, the little horn as Titus, and the one like a son of man as the King Messiah (Rashi on 7:4-8, 13). The Talmud has Rabbi Akiva read the thrones as one for God and one for David, and Rabbi Yose object (Hagigah 14a, which calls him Yose the Galilean; Sanhedrin 38b); it says the Messiah comes 'with the clouds of heaven' if Israel is worthy, and poor on a donkey if not (Sanhedrin 98a). Rashi reads the holy ones of 7:25 as Israel.
views.X: The New Testament uses this chapter more than any other passage of Daniel: Jesus calls himself the Son of Man and tells the high priest he will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand and coming on the clouds (Mark 14:62), and Revelation 4-5, 13, 17 and 20 rebuild Daniel's throne room and beasts. Hippolytus, whose commentary on Daniel (about AD 200) is the oldest surviving Christian commentary, read the beasts as Babylon, Persia, Greece and Rome, and the little horn as the Antichrist.
views.F: Readers who look to the end read the fourth beast as a final form of the Roman power, with the ten horns as ten future kings (Revelation 17:12), the little horn as the Antichrist, and the three and a half periods as the last years before Christ comes in glory. Historicists count the periods as 1,260 years and the little horn as the papacy; dispensationalists place the three and a half years in a future tribulation. Jewish readers of a future hope look to the Messiah's reign as the final kingdom.

deep.h: Daniel 2 and Daniel 7: one picture in two images
deep.b: The statue of chapter 2 and the beasts of chapter 7 describe the same course of history. Gold, silver, bronze and iron correspond to the lion, bear, leopard and the iron-toothed beast, and the stone cut without hands matches the court that takes the beast's rule and gives the kingdom to the holy ones (2:44-45; 7:26-27). The difference is in the viewpoint: the statue shows the empires as a king's image of glory, the beasts show them as monsters from the chaos sea. Both chapters allow two schemes (Babylon, Media, Persia, Greece, or Babylon, Medo-Persia, Greece, Rome), and the notes at 7:17 and 7:23 give the sources.

deep.h: What the New Testament took from this chapter
deep.b: The Gospels' 'Son of Man' sayings draw on 7:13-14 in three ways: of the Son of Man's authority on earth (Mark 2:10, 28), of his suffering and vindication (Mark 8:31; 14:62), and of his coming in glory (Mark 13:26). Acts 7:56 has Stephen see the Son of Man standing at God's right hand. Revelation joins Daniel's beasts into one (13:1-2), repeats the numbers 'ten thousand times ten thousand' (5:11), and borrows the opened books (20:12). Paul's remark that the saints will judge the world (1 Corinthians 6:2) is often linked to 7:22. Whether Jesus took the title from Daniel 7, from an expectation like that in 1 Enoch 46-71, or from the plain idiom 'a man' is debated (Casey, Dunn, Wright). See the topic on the Son of Man.

echoes: Daniel 2:31-45; Daniel 8:1-27; Daniel 9:24-27; Daniel 11:21-45; Daniel 12:1-3; Ezekiel 1:4-28; Psalm 110:1; Hosea 13:7-8; Revelation 4-5; Revelation 13:1-8; Revelation 17:7-14; Revelation 20:4-12; Mark 14:62; 1 Enoch 14; 1 Enoch 46-48; 4 Ezra 13

settings.what: Daniel's night vision of the beasts, the court and the one like a son of man
settings.by: Daniel, telling it in his own voice ('I kept looking')
settings.to: Written for the reader of the book, after Daniel wrote it down (7:1); the beasts, the court and the kingdom are shown to Daniel alone
settings.when: In the first year of Belshazzar, king of Babylon, in a dream at night
settings.why: The vision shows the course of the world's empires and ends with God's court judging the last beast and giving a kingdom to a human figure. For those who read it in trouble, it says that the monsters will lose their rule, and that the kingdom does not belong to them.
settings.readers: The vision was copied at Qumran (4QDan-a, 4QDan-b, 4QDan-d), read in Greek in two forms, rebuilt in 1 Enoch and 4 Ezra, and drawn on by Jesus and Revelation. In every century readers have placed their own enemies among the beasts.
views: Daniel himself and the exiles in Babylon, shown that Babylon and the empires after it would end and that God would give the kingdom to his holy ones.
The faithful in Judea in 167-164 BC and the teachers of the book (the maskilim of 11:33-35), shown that the horn who persecuted them would be destroyed.

settings.by: One of those standing by, an angel (7:16)
settings.to: Daniel, who asked him for the true meaning
settings.when: Right after the vision, while Daniel's spirit was troubled
settings.why: The angel gives the vision's meaning in two parts: a short one (the four kings, the holy ones receiving the kingdom, 7:17-18) and a longer one about the fourth beast and the horn, because Daniel pressed him (7:19-27). The explanation is meant to comfort: the persecutor has a fixed time, then the court sits.
settings.readers: Because the angel interprets, the identification of each beast was never fixed, and later readers, Jewish and Christian, put their own empires in the place of the beasts.
views: The explanation extended from Babylon through the kingdoms to come.
The explanation was heard as being about the horn who was making war on the holy ones now (7:21), and the 'time, times and half a time' as the time left.

traditions.q: Who is the little horn, and what is the fourth kingdom?
views: The Catechism teaches that before Christ's return the Church will pass through a final trial, and that the Antichrist is the supreme religious deception (CCC 675-677); it names no individual and does not tie the Antichrist to Daniel 7. The notes of the New American Bible, Revised Edition (the Bible of the US bishops, notes by Catholic scholars, not a doctrinal definition) say that the ten horns of 7:7-8 are Seleucid kings and the little horn is Antiochus IV Epiphanes, and that scholars disagree on whether the figure of 7:13-14 is a collective symbol or an individual such as Michael or the messiah. In the Counter-Reformation, Bellarmine and Ribera read the Antichrist as a future individual, against Reformers who read the horn as the papacy.

No Orthodox council or confession defines the little horn. The Orthodox reading comes through the fathers: Hippolytus and Cyril of Jerusalem (Catechetical Lecture 15) take the fourth beast as Rome and the little horn as the Antichrist who will appear at the end, among ten kings who divide the empire.

The Smalcald Articles (1537) declare that the pope is the very Antichrist (Part II, Article IV), without tying this to Daniel 7. Luther's Preface to Daniel, as described in studies of his eschatology, reads the fourth beast as Rome and the little horn of chapter 7 as the Turk (Mohammed's kingdom), while he keeps the pope as Antichrist elsewhere. A Lutheran reading of Daniel 7:8 is therefore not simply 'the pope'.

The Westminster Confession (25.6, 1646) says the pope is that Antichrist, man of sin and son of perdition, and the Savoy Declaration (1658, chapter 26) of the English Congregationalists repeats it; the confessions do not name Daniel 7, but historicist Reformed commentators tie the statement to the little horn. The American revision of 1788 removed the statement, and many later Reformed teachers read the horn as Rome in its first century or as a future figure. Calvin takes the fourth beast to be Rome.
The Second London Confession (26.4, 1689) repeats the Westminster wording that the pope is the Antichrist, man of sin and son of perdition; its wording does not mention Daniel.

The fourth beast is Rome and the little horn Rome in two phases, pagan and papal. The 'time, times and half a time' is 1,260 years (AD 538-1798). This is set out in Uriah Smith's Daniel and the Revelation and Ellen White's The Great Controversy.

The fourth beast is Rome in its past form and a revived form to come; the ten horns are a future alliance of ten rulers, and the little horn is the Antichrist, who persecutes Israel and the saints in the last three and a half years before Christ returns.
